subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Principle of Charity: Assume the Best Interpretation
description: Learn The Principle of Charity: Assume the Best Interpretation in one minute.

hook.text: Someone says something ambiguous. You can interpret it charitably or uncharitably. Which do you choose?

buildup.text: The principle of charity: interpret others' arguments in their strongest, most reasonable form before criticizing.

discovery.text: Donald Davidson & W.V.O. Quine: charity isn't kindness – it's a prerequisite for understanding.

twist.text: Social media destroyed charity: character limits force ambiguity, algorithms reward outrage, & tribal identity demands.

climax.text: Practice: 'What's the most reasonable thing they COULD mean?' If you can't find it, ask.

punchline.text: Assume they're reasonable until proven otherwise.

quiz.question: What is the principle of charity in argumentation?
options: Interpreting ambiguous arguments in their strongest, most reasonable form
Being nice to your debate opponent

details.summary: The principle of charity says you should interpret someone's argument in its most reasonable form before criticizing it. This prevents misunderstandings and keeps debate focused on ideas.
details.whyItMatters: Without charitable interpretation, debates degenerate into attacks on misunderstandings rather than genuine exchanges of ideas.
takeaways: Charity interprets ambiguous statements in the strongest form
It prevents straw man fallacies before they start
Charitable debate builds trust between disagreeing parties

faq.question: How does the principle of charity differ from steelmanning?
faq.answer: Charity interprets unclear statements in their most reasonable light. Steelmanning goes further by actively strengthening the argument beyond what was stated. Charity is the minimum; steelmanning is the ideal.

faq.question: When should you not apply the principle of charity?
faq.answer: When a speaker repeatedly clarifies their position and it remains weak, or when bad faith is evident. Charity applies to ambiguity, not to clearly stated poor arguments.
